title: Playing a Bolden tune through the district and tune names
summary: Passing through the district the country band played a Bolden piece to applause; he discusses unnamed band tunes and the Lizard on the Rail hit.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: You were talking about your white coats in the van there again.
And it went through the district, you said.

Through the district? Yeah. Now, we had done been made around all uptown, coming down, you know. And we had passed, we were coming through the district. That is, around Franklin Street and things. I mean, they had a place between Franklin and St. Louis. They'd run dead into the cemetery, like, you know. Around in there was all fast people, you know. You used to call it the district. So, we was coming through there late that evening, you see. Different bands had what, maybe 16, 17 bands. All they could get, they had to go in the country and get us, you know. They had money. So, we came, coming through there, we played a piece. What Bowling had made famous, you know. I don't know the name of it. How does it go? And we strong on them trumpet, too, me and my cousin, you know. And them women come out and say, yeah, come Bowling Band. They just clap for us, you know. And they just run out and say, that must be Bowling Band. Right? Our country was strong, you know. And the whole other fellas here in the city was falling out and things. We used to being in that sunny thing out there, flowering and things. We strong. We went on too.
Is that the same piece that Bowling played that you played it, you say?
Yeah. We played that in the country, yeah. You had the music for it?
You just had it. Yeah, just by air. You see, just catch them things by air. Daylight the Air. I don't remember that tune. What is it?
Sing a little more of it. Maybe I've heard it. I don't remember it, though. I don't think you heard that tune.
It was a very famous rhyme.

Yeah. That was the cornet part you were humming? Yeah. Must be Don't Go Away Nobody, huh? Don't go away nobody, huh? Don't go away nobody, huh? Don't go away nobody, huh? Don't go away nobody, huh? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. That was the cornet part you were humming? Yeah. Must be Don't Go Away Nobody, huh? It was centric too. It was centric too. It was centric too. give the tone, some of them was pretty nice pieces.
Like a blues? Huh? Like a blues, you see what it?

I mean, the band used to make their own name for the pieces. See, just like Lewis and them used to make it, called it Gut Bucket and all different kind of funny names. They had to have a name, so they just called it that name, but it was never published. You know what I'm saying? It was never published, the name or nothing. So we made a hit. And the people gave us a big hand, that band from the country, and they had a band from St. John Parish. They were good, too, at that time. I believe you should call them the Pickwick or something like that. It was pretty good. It was really nice. And the year before that, they had made a piece by the name of Howl Arthur. They made a hit with that. They had to play that. It was in the paper, you know? They played it about 20 times or something like that. It was in the daily paper. Is that there?

Is it Lizard on the Rail? Is that what I'm saying? Yeah, yeah, yeah. That's the Howl Arthur is the name of it. They just put an ad voice to it. Yeah, yeah, Lizard on the Rail. With his tail. Yeah, they made it. That's one of the Jim Mumford band he had up there, too. They made good, that was before we came in.
